transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-03-10
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Luis Garcia (Redwood SE), Nina Park (CTO, Cypher Analytics), Ravi Menon (Lead ML Eng), Elena Kozlov (SRE)

Auto Summary: (auto-generated) customer is evaluating Redwood for a low-latency streaming analytics assistant; primary focus is p95 latency, concurrency spikes, and security requirements (VPC/KMS). Agreed next steps include sending sizing worksheet and benchmark template.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, um we're Maya from Redwood, and we have Luis on the call who is our solutions engineer, how's everyone doing?
[00:07] Nina: good thanks, Nina here, sorry for the slight delay, had back-to-back, thanks for setting this up.
[00:12] Ravi: yeah hi all, Ravi on the ML infra side, looking forward, we have some pretty tight latency goals so excited to hear options.
[00:18] Elena: Elena from SRE, will be focused on networking and security bits.
[00:22] Luis: great, quick agenda: 1) understand your latency/throughput targets and traffic profile, 2) explain hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs, 3) talk about streaming and benchmarking approach, 4) next steps. sound ok?
[00:32] Nina: yep that's perfect. our core product is an analyst assistant that answers short queries and also streams long reasoning for step-by-step explainability. so two primary patterns: short responses (20-200 tokens) where p95 latency super important, and long responses (400-2000 tokens) we stream token-by-token.
[00:48] Maya: that's helpful. when you say "p95 super important" can you quantify a target?
[00:53] Ravi: for short responses we want p95 under 150ms ideally, 100ms is our stretch. concurrency during business hours averages 80-120 but we have spikes up to ~300 concurrent requests.
[01:08] Luis: ok got it. is that concurrency measured at request level or connections — are most requests streaming?
[01:13] Nina: short responses are standard request-response, not streaming. long responses are streaming and typically only a subset (~10%) of requests. connection-wise streaming holds open longer.
[01:23] Luis: makes sense. do you have an example model and context lengths? what model family are you looking at?
[01:29] Ravi: we're evaluating an open Llama-derived 8k context model, 3B-7B variants for cost reasons, sometimes larger 13B for higher quality. tokens per short request avg 80 tokens, long requests up to 1500 tokens.
[01:44] Maya: great, that helps. tradeoff note: for p95 100-150ms we usually recommend Dedicated with tuned batching and low-latency kernel selection; hosted can hit that for small scale but at spikes you'll want dedicated pools.
[01:58] Nina: ok can you explain why dedicated helps p95? is it isolation, pre-warmed instances, or specific kernel choices?
[02:06] Luis: a mix — dedicated gives you reserved GPU capacity so no cold starts, we can configure continuous batching parameters and reserve low-latency lanes. our runtime also picks kernels and compilation paths tuned for short seq lengths, and we avoid noisy neighbors.
[02:20] Ravi: how does batching affect p95? sounds like batching increases throughput but could hurt p95 if we wait to fill batches?
[02:27] Luis: exactly, it's a tradeoff. we do workload-aware batching; for strict p95 we configure maximum batch wait times (e.g., 1-3ms) and prioritize latency-sensitive traffic into smaller batches. also KV cache/prefix caching reduces tokens to generate for repeated prompts.
[02:41] Elena: for streaming long responses, do you have benchmarks for token/sec with streaming throughput? our UX streams tokens at ~20-30 tokens/sec to users, but generation should be faster on the server side to allow buffer and network delays.
[02:54] Luis: we typically measure raw tokens/sec on the GPU (server-side) — e.g., for a 7B model you might see 200-800 tokens/sec depending on quantization and sequence length; streaming introduces network/serialization overhead so end-to-end delivered token rate is lower. we size capacity to ensure headroom so user sees steady stream.
[03:12] Nina: can Redwood report p95 both at server side and end-to-end? we need to show SLA including network and any proxy latencies.
[03:20] Maya: yes we've got per-token and per-route breakdowns in the Console; you can see token-level latency, router hop time, and network e2e. for Private deployments you can integrate with your tracer if you want deeper traces.
[03:31] Ravi: about benchmarks — what's your recommended approach for us to validate 150ms p95 at concurrency 300?
[03:37] Luis: we provide a benchmark template — ideally you deploy a representative model (e.g., your 7B quantized variant) and run our generator load harness with your traffic distribution: mix of short and long, percent streaming, token lengths, and arrival pattern. we can run this on Hosted to validate and then show Dedicated pricing for same workload.
[03:51] Nina: if we run on Hosted and you see it's marginal, would Dedicated be a simple switch? how seamless are rollouts?
[03:57] Maya: yes, same API and endpoints; we can route traffic to Dedicated pool via smart routing and do canary splits. switching requires provisioning Dedicated capacity but the API and deployment config are consistent so your app code doesn't change.
[04:11] Elena: security— we need KMS integration for keys, SOC2 compliance, and audit logs. can Dedicated or Private support customer-managed KMS and HSM?
[04:19] Luis: Dedicated supports customer KMS with envelope encryption, audit logs are available in Console. Private (VPC/on-prem) gives you more control including HSM integrations. both options are SOC2-ready; we'll share the security pack.
[04:31] Ravi: latency to KMS — does KMS key unwrap impact p95? we need to ensure crypto ops aren't on the critical path for each request.
[04:39] Maya: best practice is to cache unwrapped keys in the local key cache and avoid per-request unwraps. we can walk through your KMS flow in the deep dive.
[04:47] Nina: curious about fallback if Dedicated pool saturated — what's graceful degradation look like?
[04:53] Luis: we have routing policies: burst capacity, fallback to hosted compatible model variants (e.g., lower-quality quantized variant), or queueing with a short backpressure policy. you can configure per-route SLOs to favor latency or success rate.
[05:07] Maya: customers often set a policy: keep p95 under X by falling back to smaller model for non-critical queries while preserving long-form streaming on dedicated lane.
[05:15] Ravi: for our analytics assistant, we can't degrade quality for certain query classes (regulatory compliance), so we need guaranteed capacity for those. would that be a Reserved Dedicated pool?
[05:24] Luis: yes reserved capacity with dedicated GPU pools and guaranteed throughput. we can size the pool for peak concurrency of 300 and test headroom.
[05:32] Nina: how do you size GPUs to meet 300 concurrency for short 80-token responses? is there a simple calculation?
[05:39] Luis: rough calc: measure tokens/sec per GPU for your model and quantization. short requests create more overhead per-request, so we use steady-state token rate and average tokens per second. example: if a single A100 class GPU does 50k tokens/sec for your model, and your workload is 80 tokens * 300 qps = 24k tokens/sec, so one GPU might be enough but you need headroom and consider concurrency overhead — we typically recommend >=2 GPUs for redundancy and headroom.
[06:01] Ravi: where does streaming change that math? long streaming sessions hold the session and use KV cache but average tokens/sec over time is what matters.
[06:09] Luis: right — for streaming you size to sustain average sustained tokens/sec plus handle spikes. caching lowers compute for repeated prefixes.
[06:15] Maya: i'll send a sizing workbook with a sample calculation and slot requirements.
[06:19] [07:10] (small cross talk / background noise)
[06:30] Nina: one more operational question: we run in GCP — do you offer region pinning for Dedicated or Private?
[06:35] Luis: yes, Dedicated pools can be provisioned in specific regions and Private can run in your VPC in that region. Hosted also has regional endpoints.
[06:41] Elena: about metrics retention — we need 12 months of audit logs and token-level traces for debug, is that possible?
[06:48] Maya: yes we have add-on retention packages for Console logs and you can export to your SIEM. we'll include retention pricing in the materials.
[06:55] Ravi: can we talk about quantization — are your kernels friendly to 4-bit quantization for larger models?
[07:02] Luis: yes our runtime supports 4-bit and mixed-precision paths; kernel selection picks the best path, though there are quality tradeoffs. we've got guidance for quality vs cost curves and will share recommended quant profiles.
[07:14] Nina: troubleshooting — if we see p95 regressions after rollout, how do we debug?
[07:19] Luis: Console shows per-route histograms, slow traces, and batching metrics; you can correlate with model version rollouts and infra metrics. we also have a support playbook for regression investigation.
[07:28] Maya: ok let's talk numbers — based on what you've said, short path p95 target 150ms with spikes 300 concurrency; rough cost comparison hosted vs dedicated?
[07:36] Luis: rough, Hosted is pay-as-you-go — good for validation and smaller steady load. Dedicated has monthly reserved cost but unit cost per token is lower and gives predictable latency. I'll put together a sample TCO for your profile in the sizing workbook.
[07:48] Nina: what about private? the primary reason we'd choose Private is data residency and full control; it's more up-front effort and license.
[07:55] Maya: exactly — Private is heavier lift but gives you full on-prem/VPC control, better for regulated workloads. Dedicated hits most enterprise needs with less ops burden.
[08:03] Ravi: for benchmarks, can Redwood run an internal run versus us running the harness — we'd prefer an initial Redwood-run on hosted to validate then we run dedicated tests in our environment.
[08:12] Luis: yes we can run an initial harness on hosted with your model or a close proxy; we'll anonymize and follow your data rules. then we help run dedicated sizing tests with you.
[08:20] Nina: we need to be careful with customer data; can we use a synthetic workload?
[08:24] Luis: absolutely, synthetic with the same token distribution is standard.
[08:28] Elena: networking — if we go Dedicated in our VPC, how are egress IPs and NAT handled?
[08:34] Luis: Dedicated in VPC uses customer-managed subnets and NAT/gateway per your infra; our Private option gives even tighter network control. we'll include architecture diagrams.
[08:43] [09:00] (brief pause)
[09:10] Ravi: another question on metrics — do you expose per-GPU utilization so we can see if the pool is saturated?
[09:16] Luis: yes, per-GPU metrics in Console and via API, GPU fps, memory, tokens/sec, queue lengths.
[09:22] Nina: can we route high-priority requests to a low-latency lane?
[09:26] Maya: yes, per-route SLOs and priority queues are supported; you can tag routes as critical and they get reserved capacity.
[09:32] Ravi: how quick is provisioning for Dedicated? we're aiming for a pilot in two weeks if possible.
[09:37] Luis: provisioning depends on capacity but typical is 3-10 business days for small pools; for faster pilots we can leverage hosted or pre-warm dedicated. we'll try to align with your timeline.
[09:46] Nina: timeline note — procurement wants pricing and security pack by next Friday.
[09:50] Maya: we can deliver pricing + security docs by 2026-03-12.
[09:54] Elena: thanks. any known gotchas for streaming long responses and p95? sometimes we saw server-side surges cause token bursts to slow down.
[10:02] Luis: common gotchas: underprovisioned KV cache causing regen, bursty traffic causing batch accumulation if not configured, and network serialization overhead. we recommend adding headroom in Dedicated and separate streaming lanes.
[10:15] Ravi: ok that makes sense. do you support runtime limits to preempt long-running generations so they don't block?
[10:21] Luis: yes, we have per-request timeouts and token limits, and preemption policies.
[10:26] Maya: i'll capture all these and include in the next steps.
[10:29] Nina: cool — shall we recap next actions?
[10:32] Maya: recap: 1) Maya send sizing workbook + sample TCO + security pack (by 3/12). 2) Customer to fill benchmark template and share traffic profile (by 3/16). 3) Schedule technical deep dive (Luis + infra) for region/VPC details week of 3/17. 4) Redwood to run an initial hosted benchmark if customer provides synthetic workload.
[10:50] Ravi: sounds good. one more small thing: do you have any existing customers in analytics space we can reference?
[10:55] Maya: yes we can share anonymized references — i'll include one or two names in the follow-up.
[11:00] Nina: excellent, thanks both.
[11:03] Maya: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with materials.
[11:05] (call ends)
